title: Broadband molecular dynamics simulation of fluid inertial effects in confined Brownian motion
authors: Quentin Thomas, Clara Mefo Sop, Maxime Lavaud, Yacine Amarouchene, Thomas Salez, Pascal Damman
abstract: Hydrodynamic memory governs Brownian motion over a broad range of timescales, from acoustic wave propagation at short times to diffusive relaxation at long times. While confinement-induced corrections to Brownian diffusion are well established, how confinement modifies the full hydrodynamic response remains less explored. In this Letter, we use molecular-dynamics simulations of a neutrally buoyant colloidal particle in an explicit solvent to resolve the velocity autocorrelation function across a broad hydrodynamic spectrum. In the bulk, the simulations recover compressibility, added mass, the hydrodynamic long-time tail, and Stokes-Einstein diffusion without adjustable parameters. Near a rigid wall, the velocity correlations become anisotropic, their algebraic tails are modified, and the diffusion coefficients are reduced. Most importantly, the short-time dynamics reveals a pronounced enhancement of the effective added mass as the wall is approached. As such, the velocity autocorrelation function appears as a central quantity to bridge the zero-frequency mobility and the high-frequency inertial behaviour of a confined Brownian particle.
summary: This work uses molecular dynamics simulations to study Brownian motion near a wall, focusing on the full hydrodynamic response rather than just diffusion. The key finding is that confinement modifies fluid correlations in complex ways, simultaneously suppressing low-frequency mobility while enhancing high-frequency inertial effects. This demonstrates the power of analyzing the velocity autocorrelation function across all relevant time scales.
main_problem: To investigate how fluid confinement modifies the full hydrodynamic response of Brownian motion, moving beyond established knowledge of simple diffusion corrections.
main_result: The study shows that confinement leads to anisotropic velocity correlations and reveals a counterintuitive enhancement of the effective added mass at short times as the particle approaches the wall.
method: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are used to resolve the velocity autocorrelation function across a broad hydrodynamic spectrum, linking zero-frequency mobility to high-frequency inertial behavior.
model_or_system: The system is a neutrally buoyant colloidal particle immersed in an explicit solvent and confined near a rigid planar wall. The dynamics are governed by fluid-particle interactions simulated via MD.
key_observables: Velocity Autocorrelation Function (VACF), diffusion coefficients ($D_\parallel, D_\perp$), effective added mass ($\Delta M^*$), and the hydrodynamic memory kernel.
important_parameters: Confinement distance ($\epsilon/R$), time scales ranging from acoustic to diffusive relaxation, and solvent properties (e.g., compressibility).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that MD simulations can accurately resolve the entire spectrum of fluid dynamics, validating the use of VACF as a comprehensive diagnostic tool.
figures_summary: Figures compare measured confined VACFs to theoretical predictions showing anisotropy; they also plot normalized diffusion coefficients and relative added-mass deviations against confinement ratios ($\epsilon/R$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem by reviewing hydrodynamic memory, details the MD methodology for resolving the full spectrum (bulk vs. confined), presents results on anisotropic decay rates, and quantifies both mobility suppression and inertia enhancement.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluid dynamics, the rigorous treatment of time-dependent correlations ($	ext{VACF}$) across multiple dynamic regimes—from ballistic to diffusive—is a sophisticated example of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics applicable to open quantum systems where memory effects are crucial.

Right: notations are as follows; the surface-to-surface gap ϵ, the center-to-wall distance h = ϵ + R, and the components v⊥and v∥of the colloid velocity, normal and parallel to the wall.

(b,c,d) Evolution with the colloid radius of the compressibility time τc, the added mass Ma estimated from the VACF, and the diffusion coefficient D. The solid lines correspond to the theoretical predictions as indicated.
